Based on the above statement: What are the benefits of embracing Market Price rather than Factor cost in calculating GDP? (400 Words) First Ans. The National Statistical Office under the aegis of the Ministry of Statistical and Programme Implementation is the body responsible for maintaining the National accounts. In 2015, the methodology to compute the National Income aggregates was revised. One of the changes done was to compute Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at Market Price instead of Factor Cost. The relationship between them is as follows: GDP (Market Price) = GDP (Factor Cost) + Indirect Taxes - Subsidies. The benefits of doing so are enumerated below: 1. Following the Global standard. World Bank's System of National Accounts (SNA-2008) is the global standard when it comes to National Income Accounting. By making this change, India ensures that it follows the global best practices. 2. Fair and Easy International Comparison. Due to the alignment with SNA-2008, India's macroeconomic aggregates can be easily compared with other countries. The change also ensures that the comparison is done on equal grounds. 3. More comprehensive measure Calculating GDP at Market price gives us a more comprehensive measure than calculating GDP at factor cost. This is because, Market price refers to the price that the consumers pay in the Market which is inclusive of a multitude of Production and Product taxes and subsidies. 4. Brings together the supply side and demand side estimates Since the 2015 Methodology revision, all of the data is collected sector-wise to form the Gross Value added (GVA) estimates which are calculated at basic prices. This GVA (basic prices) aggregate represents the supply side of the Indian economy. (September 2023)" - Write down the three broad methods of calculating National Income. (600 Words) First Ans. India recorded real GDP growth of 7.85% during the Apr-June period of 2023-24 as per the income or production approach, the highest in the past four quarters. As per Mody, the figure of the 7.8% GDP growth rate for the first quarter (April-June) of the financial year 2023-24 is inaccurate, and if correct calculations are applied to the data, it will come down to 4.5%. The discrepancy comes into the picture when the two series (income and expenditure) show different trends. The entire point of the discrepancy line is to acknowledge statistical imperfections, not to make them disappear. There are approaches adopted by the National Statistical Office to calculate National income are: Production or Value-added approach: - It sums the value added at each stage of production where value added is defined as total sales less the value of intermediate inputs into the production process. - Mathematically Product/Value added method = net indirect taxes + consumption of fixed capital + net value added in the primary sector at factor cost + net value added in the secondary sector at factor cost +net value added in the tertiary sector at factor cost. Income approach: - It measures the total income earned by the factors of production. Income earned by all the factors of production in an economy includes wages paid to labour, the rent earned by land, the return on capital in the form of interest, as well as corporate profits - Mathematically, Income method = net indirect taxes+ consumption of fixed capital compensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income of self-employed. Expenditure approach: - This measures the total expenditure incurred by all entities on good and services within the domestic boundaries of a country. - Mathematically, Expenditure Method = private final consumption expenditure + government final consumption expenditure + gross domestic capital formation + net export of goods and services. Ideally the growth rate in three approaches should be the same. However due to variations in data collection and processing (often referred to as statistical discrepancy) there are often gaps between the three which are taken into account while making the final calculation. Challenges with current GDP calculation methodology - Accuracy of data: The GDO calculation depends on the accuracy and credibility of the available data. Outdated data in various sectors of the economy provide an inaccurate picture of the economic activity. - Accounting unorganized sector: presently the GDO computation methodology uses data from the organized sector as a proxy for the unorganized sector. - Exclusion: Not all productive activity is included in GDP. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ **Thanks to Kingsuk bhai for framing the questions, Mridul for compiling the answers and Anmol, Anushka, Kingsuk, Krishna & Vandana for evaluating these answers. Second ans: Ashoka Mody, an economist at Princeton University, claimed in a Project Syndicate article that the National Statistical Office (NSO) did not adhere to international best practices while correcting discrepancies in its official data on income and expenditure. Mody argued that the NSO only took into account estimates of domestic income and not expenditure to calculate the growth figures, which led to overestimation of GDP growth. Mody further suggested that the correct approach would be to take into account the discrepancies in both income and expenditure approach. However, Chief Economic Advisor, V Anantha Nageswaran, and senior advisor in finance ministry, Rajiv Mishra, dismissed Mody’s claims. According to them, the approach for calculating the GDP has been consistent for years. National Income of any country means the complete value of all the goods and services produced by any country during its financial year. Therefore, it is the net result of all the economic activities that take place during a financial year and is valued in monetary terms. It includes payments made to various resources in form of rents, wages, interests, and profits. A country’s progress can be estimated by the growth of its national income. There are three broad methods of calculating national income: Value Added Method/Product Method, Income Method, and Expenditure Method. 1. Value Added Method/ Product Method: Value Added Method/ Product Method is a method of calculating the National Income of an economy in different production phases. Value Added Method/ Product Method calculates national income by evaluating the value added at each stage of production for goods and services within an economy. It measures the contribution of each industry or sector to the final product or service. Gross Value Added (GVA) is calculated by subtracting intermediate consumption (cost of goods and services used up in production) from the total output or revenue generated within a specific sector. Summation of GVA across Sectors gives us National Income. The value added by each sector (such as agriculture, manufacturing, services) is summed to obtain the GDP at factor cost. 2. Income Method: The Income Method is a method of calculating the National Income of an economy by adding up all the incomes earned by the factors of production. The factors of production include land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship. The income earned by these factors of production is known as factor income. The formula for calculating National Income through Income Method is, National Income = Rent + Wages + Interest + Profit + Mixed Income + Net Factor Income from Abroad. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ **Thanks to Kingsuk bhai for framing the questions, Mridul for compiling the answers and Anmol, Anushka, Kingsuk, Krishna & Vandana for evaluating these answers. Consumption based measurement: Using this method, poverty is estimated considering the consumption levels of households. A poverty line is estimated based on the calorie intake levels in rural and urban areas. Strengths – Consumption based measurement is considered more stable than income based measurements as consumption levels do not change as frequently as levels of income. It is also easy to understand and directly driven from the consumption patterns of individuals and also reflects their quality of life. Another important advantage is that it takes into consideration nutrition requirements. Weakness – This method is considered to take into consideration only one aspect i.e. consumption and ignoring other important aspects like health, education and various other non-monetary factors. Examples - The accepted average calorie requirement in India is 2400 calories per person per day in rural areas and 2100 calories per person per day in urban areas as defined by a task force in mid 1970s by Planning Commission. 2. Income based measurement: This method is the most common and direct way to estimate poverty be defining the minimum amount being earned by an individual in a day. Strengths – The data collection is easier in this method as compared to others because income proofs are available easily as compared to availability of proofs of consumption. Another advantage of this method is its quantitative nature. Weakness – Considering only the income of individuals is not the most appropriate way of judging the quality of life of people. Example – World Bank has defined extreme poverty headcount ration at $2.15 a day. 3. Multidimensional approach- This approach covers all three dimensions i.e. health, education and standard of living. It is further divided into indicators such as nutrition, school attendance, housing and assets, etc. Strengths – Unlike income based and consumption based approach this method focuses on more than aspect thus is not unidirectional. Y.K. Alagh Committee was formed in 1979 which recommended estimating poverty using poverty line based on nutritional requirements and consumption expenditure. 2. Lakadwala Committee of 1993 recommended state specific poverty lines and which was further divided into Consumer Price Index – Industrial Worker (CPI-IW) and Consumer Price Index – Agricultural Labour (CPI-AW) 3. Tendulkar Committee (2009) recommended shift from calorie consumption level and it also suggested uniform poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas. It also recommended new method of updating poverty lines, adjusting for changes in prices and patterns of consumption, so basically it took inflation factor into consideration. 4. Rangarajan Committee (2014) dismissed the poverty estimation method used by Tendulkar Committee and used alternate methods. It recommended poverty estimation on the basis of household survey conducted by Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE). Poverty threshold was changed to Rs 47 per day for urban areas and Rs 32 per day for rural areas. Since poverty estimation is a complex task, it requires in depth and effective methodologies to estimate poverty brackets which in turn helps researchers and policymakers to make policies which particularly target the area in which our country is lagging behind. How does the choice of poverty line impact the measurement and understanding of poverty (600 words) First ans: The estimation of the poverty line in India is a nuanced and complex process. The poverty line refers to a threshold limit that determines the number of people living in poverty. It holds immense significance and also faces many challenges in its estimation. Choosing a specific poverty line has far-reaching implications, impacting measurement and understanding of poverty. # Significance of poverty line in India: - Targeted interventions: The poverty line serves as a crucial tool in identifying and targeting a population that is needy and deprived. By identifying those in need, the government can direct resources towards issues such as education, health, and sanitation. This ensures a targeted approach to poverty alleviation and also leads to efficient utilization of public resources. - Monitoring progress: Identifying the number of people living above and below the poverty line helps us monitor our progress over the years. It enables the analysis of the impact of government interventions and policies at the ground level and ensures adjustment if needed. This fosters accountability and transparency in the fight against poverty. - International comparisons: The poverty line can help us in comparing our performance with that of other developed nations, even though there might be a few regional aspects to be considered. Such comparisons allow us to learn the best practices from other nations and also engage in the global fight against poverty. # Challenges in the estimation of the poverty line in India: - Multidimensionality: Poverty is a complex and multidimensional subject that goes far beyond income levels. Inclusion of non-consumption-based aspects of poverty, such as health, education, and sanitation, is difficult as these are not quantifiable and vary from person to person. - Dynamic needs: A static threshold may fail to capture the dynamic environmental changes, such as inflation, consumption patterns, and fluctuation in income levels. The poverty line should be regularly updated to stay relevant. - Data availability: The unavailability of accurate data poses a challenge in poverty line estimation. Collection of data from such a vast country can be difficult and expensive. - Subjectivity: Determining a minimum threshold for poverty varies in different social and cultural contexts. Even in India, poverty line estimation varies among states. This poses a challenge as it becomes difficult to consider numerous aspects and it also reduces the comparability of various poverty lines. # Impact of choice of poverty line: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ **Thanks to Kingsuk bhai for framing the questions, Mridul for compiling the answers and Anmol, Anushka, Kingsuk, Krishna & Vandana for evaluating these answers.
